ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: In an experiment in which a certain group explores Lenz's law, the group students designed the circuit shown in the figure to carry out the experiment. A fixed coil M is wound around a long straight iron core; the right end of the iron core is in close contact with a wooden cylinder; a closed metal ring N is sleeved on the wooden cylinder, and N can move without friction on the wooden cylinder. M is connected in the circuit shown in the figure, where R is a slide rheostat, E1 and E2 are DC power supplies, and S is a single-pole double-throw switch. Among the following situations, the one in which N can be observed to move to the right is (　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, in the apparatus for exploring Lenz's law, a fixed coil M is wound on a long straight iron core, the right end of the iron core is in close contact with a wooden cylinder, and a closed metal ring N that can move without friction is sleeved on the wooden cylinder. ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure, the left side is marked "left" and the right side is marked "right." A fixed coil M is wound on a long straight iron core, and coil M is located on the left; the right end of the iron core is connected to a section of wooden cylinder, and a closed metal ring N is sleeved on the wooden cylinder, with N on the right side of M. In the lower circuit, coil M is connected into a circuit containing a sliding rheostat R, DC power supplies E1 and E2, and a single-pole double-throw switch S. Switch S can connect to the upper contact a or the lower contact b. Then reason: when S is initially open, there is no current in coil M, and the magnetic flux through metal ring N is zero or unchanged. At the instant S is closed toward a, coil M is connected into a DC circuit, and the current in M begins to increase from zero; therefore the magnetic field near the right end of the iron core strengthens, and the magnetic flux through the closed metal ring N increases. According to Lenz's law, the induced current produced in N must oppose this increase in magnetic flux, so the side of N near M will form a magnetic pole of the same name as the right end of M. Adjacent like magnetic poles repel each other, and since M is on the left side of N, N is subjected to a repulsive force to the right and moves to the right.
